items.title: Clair Obscur Devs: Switch 2 Port Still "Too Early", Would Be a "Big Technical Challenge"
items.summary: Sandfall Interactive says a Nintendo Switch 2 version of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 remains interesting but unconfirmed, citing Unreal Engine 5 limitation
items.content:
Sandfall Interactive has again declined to confirm a Nintendo Switch 2 version of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, with studio CEO and creative director Guillaume Broche telling Automaton West it remains “too early” to announce anything, while co-founder and CTO Tom Guillermin warned that squeezing the acclaimed RPG onto Nintendo’s hybrid would be a “big technical challenge.”

The comments came in a newly published interview with the Japan-focused outlet, in which the pair, alongside lead character and concept artist Alan Reynaud and technical artist Alexandre Breton, discussed the studio’s post-launch plans roughly a year after the game’s breakout release. Asked directly whether Expedition 33 could run on Switch 2, Broche replied: “We are interested in looking for a way to do it, but it’s too early for us to announce anything at this point.”

Pressed on why a port isn’t straightforward, Guillermin pointed to the hardware gap between Nintendo’s console and the platforms Expedition 33 already runs on. “It’s a big technical challenge because we tried to do something beautiful with the game, but of course, the Switch 2 is not as powerful as the PlayStation or the Xbox Series X ,” he said, adding that the studio has to weigh this “especially given the size of our studio.”

That caveat matters: Expedition 33 was built by a small, largely first-time development team at Sandfall, a detail the studio has repeatedly stressed when discussing the resources needed for new platform work.

The engine underpinning the game adds a further wrinkle. Asked whether Unreal Engine 5 itself complicates a Switch 2 build, Broche said simply: “Yes, a lot of features don’t work on Switch 2.” Reynaud, however, floated one possible way forward, noting that Epic Games’ newer Lumen Lite lighting option could eventually ease that burden even though the rollout takes time. “They’re introducing features like Lumen Lite now, which is easier to run than the standard Lumen, but these things take time to roll out, so we’ll have to consider the updates coming from Unreal Engine to determine what to do,” he said.

Nintendo Everything, which independently reported on the same Automaton West interview, confirmed the quoted exchange and noted that Unreal Engine 5.8 began rolling out about a month earlier, bringing Lumen Light, with Epic Games indicating it would be pretty impactful for Nintendo Switch 2. Niche Gamer, covering the same remarks separately, observed that the level of detail in the developers’ answer suggests the studio “has certainly put effort and consideration into a port,” even as no commitment has been made.

Sandfall has fielded the Switch 2 question repeatedly since before the console even launched. Back in May 2025, Broche told another interviewer that the game’s runaway success “changes everything” for the studio’s options, while stopping short of confirming a port. By September 2025, Sandfall’s official line had firmed up only slightly, with the team stating it had “some opportunities that we will explore, but currently we cannot confirm anything.”

Niche Gamer summed up the frustration many fans feel: the game is “the 2025 Game of the Year and currently the highest-rated user score release of all time on Metacritic,” yet more than a year after launch there is still no word on a Switch 2 port. Expedition 33 debuted on PC, PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X/S in April 2025 and has never been available on any Nintendo platform, base Switch included, despite third-party heavyweights like Cyberpunk 2077 and Hogwarts Legacy making the jump to Switch 2.

The persistence of the question isn’t surprising given Switch 2’s early trajectory. The console has already sold in the tens of millions worldwide since its mid-2026 launch window, a scale that makes any unported acclaimed RPG a conspicuous gap in the library for Nintendo-only players in markets including New Zealand and Australia, where the base Switch’s install base remains large and Switch 2 stock has been in steady demand.

For now, Sandfall’s position hasn’t shifted from “interested but unconfirmed.” Whether Lumen Lite, further Unreal Engine updates, or simply more development time change that calculus is something only the studio can answer — and, as Broche reiterated to Automaton West, it isn’t ready to do so yet.

items.title: Clair Obscur Dev Still Interested In Switch 2 Port, But Admits It Would Be A "Big Technical Challenge"
items.content:
The French Studio behind the award-winning role-playing title Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 has already discussed the idea of a Switch 2 port, so what's the latest update on this?

In an interview with Automaton recently , Sandfall Interactive's CEO and creative director Guillaume Broche reiterated how the studio was still "interested" in getting a Nintendo version of the Unreal Engine 5 game up and running. However, it's still "too early" for the team to officially announce or confirm anything.

Co-founder Tom Guillerman admits a Switch 2 version is a "big technical challenge", and Sandfall has to consider this given the smaller size of the studio , which called on external support during the game's development.

Broche added how "a lot of features don't work on Switch 2", but lead character and concept artist Alan Reynaud highlighted how features such as "Lumen Lite" are now being made available, so the team will have to consider the updates rolling out for Unreal Engine to determine its next steps.

Our colleagues at Push Square called Clair Obscur a daring, quirky and absolute must-play RPG when it launched last year.

items.title: Clair Obscur devs talk up possible Switch 2 port
items.summary: If the 2025 Game of the Year Award Winner, Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is coming to Switch 2, it won’t come easily.
items.content:
Though rumors have rumbled for a possible Nintendo Switch 2 port for developer Sandfall Interactive’s Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , the 2025 Game of the Year and currently the highest-rated user score release of all time on Metacritic, we’re well over a year since the game’s initial release with no word on a Switch 2 port.

Notable leaker NateTheHate shared his confidence in a Switch 2 release back in June, so take that for what it’s worth. If you’d like a more official confirmation that Clair Obscur could be bound for the Nintendo system, you’d likely be interested in a recent interview conducted between the developers and Automation Media.

Between questions revolving around the developers’ inspirations, opinions on what being a Japanese role-playing game actually means, and gameplay style preferences, the team was questioned on what it would take to get the massively popular release to the booming Switch 2 console.

Their response communicated that bringing a visual and technical masterstroke to a technically inferior system would be incredibly challenging, but the detail within their answer suggests one key truth: they’ve certainly put effort and consideration into a port.

For Switch 2 owners, that’s probably all you needed to know to feed your optimism.

Here’s a direct quote from Automation Media’s interview.

Question: I think your fans are quite curious about a Switch 2 version. Do you think Expedition 33 would be able to run on the Switch 2? And do you have any such plans at the moment?

Guillaume Broche: We are interested in looking for a way to do it, but it’s too early for us to announce anything at this point.

Tom Guillermin: It’s a big technical challenge because we tried to do something beautiful with the game, but of course, the Switch 2 is not as powerful as the PlayStation or the Xbox Series X. So, it’s an important thing for us to consider, especially given the size of our studio.

Question: Do you think Unreal Engine 5 is also a challenge when trying to bring Expedition 33 to the Switch 2?

Guillaume Broche: Yes, a lot of features don’t work on Switch 2.

Alan Reynaud: They’re introducing features like Lumen Lite now, which is easier to run than the standard Lumen, but these things take time to roll out, so we’ll have to consider the updates coming from Unreal Engine to determine what to do.

Staff writer at Niche Gamer. Calvin lives in Japan, but is originally from the USA. When he's not writing, he's wringing his copy of Mario Kart World for every penny it's worth.

items.title: After Clair Obscur Expedition 33, Sandfall Interactive is "going to go a bit crazy" with its next game: "We want to let ourselves dream again and be creative"
items.summary: Expedition 33 was quite a long project too
items.content:
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .

(Image credit: Sandfall Interactive) Copy link Facebook X Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 1 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter We won't see a new game from Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 studio Sandfall Interactive for a few years, it seems, but the studio's leaders are confident it will be something "a bit crazy."

Speaking with Automaton , Sandfall CEO Guillaume Broche reexamines the studio's plans for its next game – only its second release after the breakout success of Expedition 33, which was largely made by a team of junior staff.

"It's too early to say anything precise, but we had a lot of fun creating Expedition 33, and it's a game that we all love internally, so we want to find this flame, this passion again for the next project," Broche says.

"Expedition 33 was quite a long project too. Especially for me, it was six years. For Tom it was five and a half, and for most of the other members it was between four and five years. That's also why we want to let ourselves dream again and be creative again. We're going to go a bit crazy."

Don't interpret that craziness as a massively inflated scope, however. Broche affirms that Sandfall wants to stay small. Currently, the studio has around 26 people, which he calls "more than enough" for pre-production on the next game. If they cracked open the Expedition 33 war chest and hired a ton of people to make a gigantic game, Broche reckons they'd lose part of the team's charm.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 lead doesn't "care" if his next game isn't as popular as the GOTY RPG Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 devs were told that "no one" would like one of the RPG's best systems Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 lead says we'll eventually "be able to churn out a game" with a prompt "If we know we can't do everything, we have to focus on what matters, and I think that philosophy is what made Expedition 33 what it is," he says. "It feels very focused, everything has a purpose, and everything is made for a reason. It doesn’t feel like something too big for its own good."

Earlier this year, Broche commented on the second album syndrome facing whatever game follows Expedition 33. Unbothered by sales comparisons or critical expectations, he said "we're just going to do what we love again" as "we didn't make the first game to please anyone" and that worked out pretty alright.

Sandfall staff have said as much since the end of the GOTY season that saw Expedition 33 showered in trophies. COO and production director François Meurisse likewise said the team's next game will just focus on "what we think is cool," not what's expected to perform or, as writer Jennifer Svedberg-Yen put it, "please a lot of people."

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Director Says End Of Physical Discs Is ‘Super Sad’
items.summary: The devs also revealed that their publisher discussed skipping physical, but figured players would want to 'hold it in their hands'
items.content:
Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 Physical Games PS5 Sandfall

Earlier this month, PlayStation announced that it would end production of physical video game discs in a few years . This led to a lot of shouting, calls to boycott the company, and more. And the devs behind last year’s hit game Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 recently explained that while they understand the “business” reasons for the decision, it is still “a shame” that discs are going away.

In a new interview with Automaton , as part of a larger post-mortem event, some devs from Clair Obscur studio Sandfall talked about last year’s indie (?) super hit . But the team was also asked about the recent news that PlayStation was ending physical disc production of new video games starting in 2028. For them, it’s sad news as they find physical games to be “special” and important to players.

“Personally, I find it super sad because I really like video game stores,” said creative director Guillaume Broche. “And even if nowadays, I play mainly on PC myself, we have a lot of people on the team who play on PS5 and love to collect physical discs. I think it’s part of the beauty of art too—that it’s something tangible that you can touch. I completely appreciate that people want to have their rows of DVDs and games and just feel that they own them. So I think it’s a shame.”

Broche added that while it makes sense “business-wise,” in terms of the “artistry of video games, it’s a sad decision.”

Sandfall co-founder and CTO Tom Guillermin shared an interesting story regarding Expedition 33 ‘s own physical edition. Before the release of the game, there were discussions about not doing a physical release. Physical releases add more complications to the process of making and selling a video game, and cutting it can save a lot of money. But for Sandfall, it sounds like it was never a real option. Guillermin said that “physical was something special” for the studio, and that the team wanted players to be able to “hold [the game] in their hands.”

“So even though it made things harder and meant less money per unit,” said Guillermin, “it was important for us to provide players who want to have the physical game in their hands with an option. Because that’s what we value as players too.”

The devs also shared that walking into a store and seeing physical copies of their game made it feel “real.” And that was true of other games, not just their own.

“Knowing that may not be possible again makes me a bit sad,” said lead character and concept artist Alan Reynaud. “And maybe it’s the child in me, but I like to go outside, buy a game, and come back home with it. It’s a nice feeling.”

“ I think the same principle can apply to manga. It’s nice to read on your phone and stuff, but having a real book is just a different feeling. And I don’t think we could imagine a world where manga is just scanned and stored on your computer. It would be sad to not have it in your library. I think the same applies for games. Sure, it makes more sense business-wise, but you lose the spirit of it.”

The Sandfall team isn’t alone in their love of physical media and their concerns for what it could mean for the future. But it seems extremely unlikely that Sony changes its plans at this point, especially when you consider how few physical games are sold compared to digital. The all-digital future is coming , and unfortunately it doesn’t seem like Sony or Xbox are ready for it. You can read more of Automaton ‘s interview with the Expedition 33 team here.

items.title: "It's a sad decision." Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developers on the end of physical disc production and why they pushed for a physical release despite the drawbacks
items.summary: Interview with Sandfall Interactive's core members about what physical games mean to them.
items.content:
Home Interviews “It’s a sad decision.” Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 developers on the end of physical disc production and why they pushed for a physical release despite the drawbacks Interview with Sandfall Interactive's core members about what physical games mean to them.

Interviews 2026-07-29 00:01 Genki Epic Games Japan and Sandfall Interactive recently hosted a Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem event in Yokohama, Japan, where the developers shared technical insights into the making of 2025’s Game of the Year. Following the event, AUTOMATON sat down with the team and took the opportunity to ask about their thoughts on physical game releases. With PlayStation set to end game disc production in 2028, the developers briefly reflected on why they insisted on releasing Expedition 33 physically despite the added challenges, and discussed why they believe physical editions remain important to video games as a medium.

Guillaume Broche – Sandfall Interactive CEO and Creative Director Tom Guillermin – Sandfall Interactive Co-founder and CTO Alan Reynaud – Lead Character and Concept Artist Alexandre Breton – Technical Artist

For more about Sandfall Interactive’s Japanese influences, thoughts on Unreal Engine, and studio upsizing, check out part one of this interview .

— PlayStation recently announced that it will end physical disk production in 2028. What are your thoughts on that?

Guillaume Broche: Personally, I find it super sad because I really like video game stores. And even if nowadays, I play mainly on PC myself, we have a lot of people on the team who play on PS5 and love to collect physical discs. I think it’s part of the beauty of art too – that it’s something tangible that you can touch. I completely appreciate that people want to have their rows of DVDs and games and just feel that they own them. So I think it’s a shame. I mean, business-wise, I can understand why it may make sense, but I think in terms of the artistry of video games, it’s a sad decision.

Tom Guillermin: In our discussions with our publisher prior to the release of Expedition 33, the question of whether or not to do a physical release cropped up. A physical release adds more constraints because you have to account for the production time of the physical items, and you also earn less money per copy.

But for us, physical was something special. We also felt that the game could be special to players, and that they would want to, as Guillaume said, hold it in their hands.

So even though it made things harder and meant less money per unit, it was important for us to provide players who want to have the physical game in their hands with an option. Because that’s what we value as players too.

Guillaume Broche: To add to that, there were two very strong moments when the game released. After launch, we went to a video game store to buy our own game (laughs). Just as a gesture. And another strong memory I have is when someone from Japan sent me a picture [of our game] from a video game store – in Akihabara I think – in Japanese writing and all. I felt like a kid when I saw it. I was like “Yeah, it’s real!” It starts feeling real when you see it in stores. Alan Reynaud: Even now when I’m going to the supermarket or something, if I see our game in a store, it always makes my day. It’s a bit selfish, because it’s our game, but it always makes me go “Oh!”

Knowing that may not be possible again makes me a bit sad. And maybe it’s the child in me, but I like to go outside, buy a game, and come back home with it. It’s a nice feeling.

Alexandre Breton: And it’s not just because it’s “our game.” I think what’s cool [about physical games in general] is that a few years later, you’ll have your box, and you can hold it and look at the title and remember all the memories that are linked to the game.

Alan Reynaud: I think the same principle can apply to manga. It’s nice to read on your phone and stuff, but having a real book is just a different feeling. And I don’t think we could imagine a world where manga is just scanned and stored on your computer. It would be sad to not have it in your library. I think the same applies for games. Sure, it makes more sense business-wise, but you lose the spirit of it.

Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is available for PC ( Steam ), PS5 and Xbox Series X|S.

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 director says eliminating limitations in development is a "big mistake." We talk to Sandfall Interactive about staying small, Japanese influences, and what's next
items.summary: Interview with Sandfall Interactive at the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem in Yokohama, Japan.
items.content:
Home Interviews Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 director says eliminating limitations in development is a “big mistake.” We talk to Sandfall Interactive about staying small, Japanese influences, and what’s next Interview with Sandfall Interactive at the Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem in Yokohama, Japan.

Game Development , Interviews 2026-07-29 00:00 Genki Epic Games Japan and Sandfall Interactive recently hosted a Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 postmortem event in Yokohama, Japan, offering a behind-the-scenes look at the development of 2025’s Game of the Year. After the presentation, AUTOMATON sat down with the developers to discuss their Japanese influences, their views on JRPGs, why Unreal Engine was the right choice for their small team, and why the studio has no intention of significantly increasing its headcount.

Participants are as follows: Guillaume Broche – Sandfall Interactive CEO and Creative Director Tom Guillermin – Sandfall Interactive Co-founder and CTO Alan Reynaud – Lead Character and Concept Artist Alexandre Breton – Technical Artist

For more about Sandfall Interactive’s views on physical disc production ending , check out part two of this interview.

—Could you tell me about the influence Japanese games and anime have had on your approach to game design? What were some of the biggest Japanese influences on Expedition 33?

Guillaume Broche: Growing up, I’d say 95% of the games I was playing were Japanese games, so I’ve always been super influenced by them. My first real video game memory was Final Fantasy VIII on PS1. Before that, I’d also played some games on the Mega Drive, but they were smaller titles and I don’t remember them very well because I was too young. But to this day, JRPGs in particular continue to be one of my favorite genres.

And of course, one of the main influences in my life is the Final Fantasy series and the work of Hironobu Sakaguchi, including titles like Lost Odyssey and Blue Dragon. Other JRPGs that have influenced me include the Shin Megami Tensei and Persona series, the Atelier series, and Tales of Vesperia. I’ve said it a million times by now, but I pretty much play almost all JRPGs available at the time. Not every single one, but really a lot.

Obviously, Expedition 33’s gameplay is very much inspired by the older Final Fantasy games. It’s turn-based, and you have three characters facing three monsters, so they were definitely a massive inspiration.

Also, as I grew up, I think I’d been missing that kind of game ever since Lost Odyssey. Lost Odyssey was, for me, the last big realistic turn-based game. You still have titles like Yakuza and Persona coming out now, but they’re more stylized. On the other hand, I felt like the grand, epic, realistic kind of turn-based games like Final Fantasy X and Last Odyssey didn’t exist anymore. Since that’s my favorite type of game personally, I just wanted to make it.

—How about anime? I believe you’ve mentioned being a big Ghibli fan, but have you drawn influence from any specific titles?

Guillaume Broche: Yes, I know that for a lot of people in the West, Disney is a big part of their childhood memories, but for me, it’s Ghibli. Especially Spirited Away. I think I’ve seen that movie 50 times, no joke. It’s a masterpiece from A to Z, and I also love other films by the studio.

Also, I think one of the anime that inspired me for Expedition 33’s story was Attack on Titan. I really like the idea of a group of heroes fighting together, and I especially love the uniform. When you see any character from Attack on Titan, you instantly know they’re an Attack on Titan character because of the uniform. That’s something I really wanted to bring over into Expedition 33, making the game recognizable just from its uniforms.

In fact, I’m rewatching Attack on Titan right now because I haven’t watched it for at least six years. I’m on season four now, almost at the end, and really, it’s an absolute masterpiece for me.

Alan Reynaud: For the characters, there were a lot of anime that had a big influence on us. One of them is Bleach. I have to mention Bleach because the character designs in the series are spectacular. One of the things we took from it was designs that are super simple yet incredibly memorable. We wanted to have something like that, with a “rule of cool” approach. I’d say that was a big inspiration for the character creation.

items.title: Clair Obscur Isn't The Only Great RPG That's Cheaper Right Now
items.summary: These are the current role-playing game deals I'd recommend
items.content:
It’s summer backlog season. What better way to celebrate than by adding a few more games to the list? A bunch of role-playing games are on sale for PS5 right now , including some heavy hitters that only came out last year like Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 .

PlayStation just refreshed its summer sale, which doesn’t end until August 13 . Here are some of the RPGs you can currently save a bunch on (assuming you don’t already own them):

Kingdom Come: Deliverance 2 and Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 are both must-plays that haven’t gotten cheaper than this, though if you aren’t interested or already own them, $40 is a decent price for the very meaty, numbers-intensive Digimon Story Time Stranger.

The above are all easy-to-recommend games, especially for the genre and their current respective discount levels. But if you want my real RPG sicko picks, I’d also recommend the following:

I’ll explain each pick briefly. .hack//G.U. Last Recode is an HD remaster of the original PS2 trilogy which CyberConnect2 recently revealed will be making a comeback with a new game in a few years. The DioField Chronicle is a neat, top-down real-time strategy hybrid RPG that Square Enix should have never made but I have a big soft spot for. Resonance of Fate is a bizarro PS3-era RPG from Tri-Ace that has a really cool hybrid action combat system with guns. Persona 3 Portable is an isometric demake that plays more like a point-and-click visual novel but is perfect for Persona fans who want a more old-school-feeling version of the game.

items.title: The Combat in These 8 Open-World Games Games Puts Clair Obscur: Expedition 33's to Shame
items.summary: There's little wrong with Clair Obscur's combat, but these titles give it a run for its money.
items.content:
By Harry Ted Sprinks Published Jul 26, 2026, 10:30 AM EDT Sign in to your DualShockers account Add Us Summary Generate a summary of this story Like Like follow Follow followed Followed Thread 2 Log in Here is a fact-based summary of the story contents: Try something different: Show me the facts Explain it like I’m 5 Give me a lighthearted recap Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 has become a celebrated release in the RPG genre, beloved for its dynamic turn-based combat, unique setting, and captivating narrative. Its combat is notable, and there's certainly little wrong with it.

Discover the many grand adventures that remain stuck in the past.

However, for those looking for more or perhaps something radically different in an open-world setting, there's plenty on offer. From the lightning-quick combat of Sunset Overdrive to the slow and deliberate challenges of Elden Ring, there's something for everyone if you want to try something different from Clair.

Expand Collapse Look, Kingdom Come: Deliverance isn't for everyone. In fact, it's not a game for me. But that doesn't take away from the fact that its combat system can be tremendously rewarding.

The reason for this is that Kingdom Come: Deliverance can be brutal. Combat is tough and players shouldn't expect to take on multiple opponents and get away unscathed, if alive at all. But have patience, learn its systems, and Kingdom Come: Deliverance can be worthwhile. However, its combat is delivered in a unique and sometimes clunky way, and some may bounce off of it quite quickly.

Expand Collapse Some players may consider Fallout: New Vegas to have a somewhat antiquated combat system. Its gunplay and melee combat can be a little clunky. However, the VATs system, RPG mechanics, and diverse arsenal of weapons allow for deep and satisfying gameplay.

In addition, Fallout: New Vegas can be incredibly tactical; the game often requires careful positioning and threat assessment in order to succeed. Combined with its expansive open world and plethora of unique side-quests, Fallout: New Vegas is a must-play.

Expand Collapse While perhaps not a true open-world game, Destiny 2's many zones can be freely explored by the player. In essence, the opportunities for exploration that it provides are similar to that of smaller open world games. 'Open World' is also a popular user-defined tag for the game on its Steam store page.

Semantics aside, Destiny 2 is perfect for players that enjoy good combat and open-world exploration. As an FPS, Destiny 2 focuses on gunplay above all else, and here it passes with flying colors. Any fan of sci-fi, exploration, and FPS combat should certainly give Destiny 2 ago.

No Rest for the Wicked Action RPG Hack and Slash Soulslike Open-World

Expand Collapse Although it falls somewhat short with its emphasis on farming/grinding and the addition of in-game timers, No Rest For The Wicked makes up for this with its combat system. No Rest For The Wicked is an ARPG with elements of a Soulslike. More specifically, it blends Soulslike combat with the structure of an ARPG.

Nothing beats being a wizard with complete freedom.

This combat is weighty, challenging, and allows for real mastery. And, while the aforementioned emphasis on farming might not be my cup of tea, it does allow players to better prepare themselves for more challenging foes.

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 & the Beauty of a Non-Definitive Ending
items.summary: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 gives Maelle and Verso two painful endings. This feature examines grief, escapism, and why neither choice is wrong.
items.content:
Imagine: it’s PAX West 2025, and you’re me, wandering the expo hall with hundreds if not thousands of others. It’s a sea of people, but amongst them, you start to notice an incredibly peculiar pattern: dotting the crowd are bright red French berets. You cross direct paths with someone and notice their red beret is not only accompanied by a black-and-white striped shirt, but a red checked sash, strapping a fake plastic baguette to their back. You’re immediately both intrigued and perplexed, and raise the obvious question to your partner, who explains it’s from that game he started playing “with Charlie Cox in it”.

In this scenario, you are very much a fan of Charlie Cox and his starring in Daredevil, so you’re immediately reminded of what he’s talking about in that explanation – Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. You vaguely remember seeing the first casting announcement trailer for it during a random State of Play one early morning and getting excited because Daredevil(!), but ultimately you ended up going back to your endless, hellish cycle of Marvel Rivals lobbies when the game actually released. The red berets are a kind reminder of your previous excitement about the game, though, and it isn’t long after that you find yourself glued to your television while being serenaded by a beautiful French accent as you are formally introduced to the citizens of Lumiere. Your four years of French classes throughout school surely prepared you for this moment.

What you aren’t prepared for is just how much of an effect this game has on you by the end.

Now, at the risk of being honest, it’s a complete understatement to say I love this game. If you have interacted with me within the last year, I have talked to you about this game, or I have told you to finish it after you told me you didn’t even get through Act I, or I have endlessly gushed over Lorien Testard’s soundtrack what was probably an annoying amount. It’s rare to find yourself so committed to a piece of media, if only because you see yourself reflected in it so wholly, whether it’s in Maelle’s escapism or Verso’s self-sacrificial tendencies. After all, you don’t win 37 awards because people just feel pretty okay emotions about your game. As is with any piece of media, though, comes what others have to say about it.

(Obligatory note: What’s discussed going forward is riding off of the notion that the person reading this has played the game. If you haven’t, maybe go open Steam or the PlayStation store, grab some tissues, strap in for a bit, and hopefully you will thank me later. Or feel free to keep reading – I’m certainly not stopping you).

One of the gaming community’s most divisive conversations regarding Expedition 33 is regarding the two distinct endings the game has to offer, notwithstanding how both are unique in how they highlight the game’s central theme around the idea of grief. There hasn’t been a day that’s gone by in recent memory where I haven’t been faced with someone explaining how “[insert your preferred character’s name] ending is the right one”, or “if you chose [insert your not-preferred character’s name] ending, you’re clearly heartless”.

In the first ending, the audience is brought back to Lumiere after Maelle and Verso’s battle, and we see that Maelle has not erased the canvas, which was her motivation by the end of Act III. We’re rejoined by the ensemble we’ve grown to love, the Expeditioners as well as Esquie and Monoco, and we even see that Gustave and Sophie have both been repainted after their previous deaths. We’re also faced with Maelle and a considerably older Verso. We see Verso struggle for an uncomfortable moment, his hands stretching out and freezing over keys of a grand piano in Lumiere’s opera house, until it can be discerned Maelle uses her Paintress abilities in order to force the painted version of her late brother to play.

The colors are washed. The lighting is dimmed. It doesn’t yield much comfort aside from the embrace of familiar faces, but that just might be enough.

The second ending is an intentionally stark contrast. For the first time in the game, we’re officially brought outside of the canvas now that it’s presumably been destroyed, as that was Verso’s desire by the end game, and we’re shown the Dessendre’s. In front of them sits a grave donning the name “Verso Dessendre”. Renoir and Aline share a tender embrace in front of their son’s grave, Clea leaves behind a bouquet of achingly familiar red and white flowers before excusing herself, and we see a scarred Alicia– or Maelle– standing by as she watches the scene unfold, holding a sewn Esquie doll. The camera turns and we see the images of the very same Expeditioners, including Gustave and Verso’s painted self, framed by the Eiffel Tower as they wave goodbye before dissipating.

The colors are bright. It’s backlit by a sunny day. The comfort is uncertain and bittersweet, but it’s ultimately not an unwelcome feeling, either.

Undeniably, the discussion around these endings is, of course, typically viewed as black-and-white as possible. More often than not, when faced with multiple endings by the end of a game, audiences are used to getting a “good” ending and a “bad” ending, leaving little room for discussion. And, in these cases, that is the game’s intent. In these cases, the games do have a black-and-white, a good-and-bad. It’s not unheard of for a game to punish a player for making poor choices throughout a play through. When looking at Expedition 33’s endings, though, this mindset is frankly doing a disservice to the game’s theming as a whole.

Grief as a theme is interwoven throughout the entire game, and when is the process of grieving ever black-and-white? Grief by all accounts is an incredibly non-linear process. We have all grieved over someone, over something, and we all understand what that means. Both of the endings evoke very different emotions, but it really is up to the player and what they choose to prioritize within their own grief. Yes, in Maelle’s ending, we see the way she chooses to use her Paintress abilities against her brother and father’s wishes, but more importantly, she’s also surrounded by those she has come to love, in a fully-functioning body. She’s given grace to those who have only ever lived inside of the canvas, reasserting the idea that they are sentient individuals with their own lives and autonomy, despite the circumstances they were painted into. Within Verso’s ending, the Dessendre’s are now able to work on moving past their shared grief regarding the loss of their real-life brother and son after years of stagnation, but at the cost of Alicia having a healthy physical body, and at the loss of everyone we have come to love inside of the canvas.

Both of these endings offer a resolution and catharsis in their own ways, and the outcome of one doesn’t make the other more or less right. When discussing these endings, we can’t assume why someone chose one ending over the other, because their grief surrounding the game is ultimately their own, and it’s not up to us to dictate how that feels to them. It can’t be stressed enough how sacrificing nuance in these discussions doesn’t only do a disservice to the game, but also the players and their own emotions about it.

I have a confession to make: I wholeheartedly chose Maelle’s ending the first time I played, and at that moment, it wasn’t a difficult choice for me. It made sense. I had grown so incredibly fond of Lumiere and the canvas and those inside of it, just like Maelle, but I saw myself in so many facets of her. I was a sixteen-year-old girl once, finding escape in worlds I created and in the media I was in love with, be it novels or games or movies, in order to remove myself from the very real grief I was experiencing. It’s something I still find myself doing even in adulthood, and ironically, probably the reason why I found myself so absorbed in Expedition 33 in the first place. The hours I put into the game were the direct result of me needing a distraction from life, and to watch the game slowly begin to unveil what it truly was felt like looking into a mirror. Of course I chose to save Lumiere. Of course I sided with Maelle. It’s what I do all the time. More often than not, I run from my grief rather than let myself feel it, and instead I look for reassurance and acceptance and comfort in worlds where my real feelings can’t hurt me. It’s far easier to feel for the characters on my screen than it is to feel for myself. After all, their emotions aren’t tangible, unlike my own. Expedition 33 was the first time I had ever personally experienced a piece of media that conveyed that feeling in a way that felt so specific, and so undeniably real.

items.title: Clair Obscur is flawed on purpose, says director: 'Games that try to be perfect, that try to fix all their flaws—they're usually just really boring'
items.content:
When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works .

(Image credit: Kepler / Sandfall Interactive) Copy link Facebook X Whatsapp Reddit Pinterest Flipboard Email Share this article 11 Join the conversation Follow us Add us as a preferred source on Google Newsletter Subscribe to our newsletter Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 , in my humble opinion, deserves the laurels it got—it's a gorgeous, inventive, personality-filled romp with an ending that rips your heart out and stomps it into a pulp fine enough for use in paint. But I'd hesitate to call it 'perfect', mostly because I don't believe in perfection as a concept, but also because there were a few moments where it lost me—like those freaking mimes . Hate those guys.

Anyway, in a recent interview with the YouTube channel Konbini , creative director Guillaume Broche says that—among a lot of other inspirations—he was inspired by games with clear and glaring imperfections, jokingly referencing the infamous Devil May Cry scene where Dante screams: "I should've been the one to fill your dark soul with light!"

"I think these games are really endearing," says Broche. "You see their flaws and think to yourself, 'yeah, it's lame, but I don't care. It's part of the character's flaws, and that's what makes them'. You're not looking for a perfect game. A perfect game is boring anyway."

As a matter of fact, Broche has a theory of perfection that games with a bit of jank are better than games that try to cover them up: "Games that try to be perfect, that try to fix all their flaws—they're usually just really boring."

Watch On Generally speaking, I couldn't agree more—neither could my colleagues, who are often ardent defenders of eurojank : "My theory is that it's just like people. People who try to be perfect are boring because they have no personality. Whereas people who embrace their slightly weird side—in the end, are the interesting ones."

Andy Serkis says 'there has always been that snobbery' when it comes to videogame acting, but the times are changing thanks to games like Expedition 33 Brigador devs think it's crucial that their abrasive, hardcore mech sims aren't for everyone: 'I think we make boy slop, but that's okay' 'I do think Blow misunderstood what the game is about': Derelict Star made Jonathan Blow rage quit, but it's the most fascinating indie platformer I've played for years As far as the purposeful jank that made it into Clair Obscur, Broche brings up its intentionally-obnoxious minigames: "We knew when we were making them: it was going to be unbearable, people were going to lose it, but it's part of the fun. We thought it was funny. And, well, it's imperfect, but whatever—we're putting it in.

"With Clair Obscur, there are plenty of design decisions that are fundamentally flawed. What we heard a lot before we released the game was: You're making a game that mixes the challenging aspects of an action game—with dodging and parrying—with turn-based gameplay. No-one's going to like it."

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

I liked it quite a lot, but I'm both an RPG-lover and a parry fanatic , so Clair Obscur was so deeply designed for me it felt almost targeted. Still, Broche admits, "fundamentally there are a lot of design decisions [in Clair Obscur] that, from an outside or business perspective, make no sense at all."

items.title: Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 is now available in Arabic!
items.summary: Expeditioners! Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text! This brings the total number of supported langua
items.content:
Expeditioners!

Following the huge demand from so many of you, we’ve been working super hard to be able to finally announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33, is now available with Arabic text!

This brings the total number of supported languages to 20!

With the new Arabic language support, we had to consider additional changes to the game’s UI to ensure a smooth and enjoyable experience for Arabic-speaking players around the world.

Adding Arabic localization has been a true team effort over many months, from the incredible adaptation and localization work carried out by the linguists, to reworking the vast majority of the user interface for right-to-left reading, all the way through localization testing.

Every team involved brought passion and dedication to making this possible, and we couldn’t be more grateful for their work. We hope this update makes the story feel even more personal to our players.

Today’s update also includes some additional fixes and improvements. Read the full patch notes here!

Thank you all so much for your continued support! <3

Tomorrow comes.

~ The Expedition 33 Team

items.title: 1st Anniversary of Clair Obscur: Expedition 33
items.summary: Expeditioners!! Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special
items.content:
Expeditioners!! 

 

Today marks 1 year since we released Clair Obscur: Expedition 33. This past year has been an incredible journey and so we have a few things to share with you today. 

 

To celebrate the occasion, the team put together a special piece of artwork that we hope you will enjoy! 

8 Million Copies Sold

We're so thrilled, and honestly still quite overwhelmed, to announce that Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 has officially reached 8 million copies sold!

Thank you so so much to every single person who has played, created art, shared, streamed, discussed, and supported this game!!

Game Update: New Haircuts + Patch Notes

We've pushed a fun little update live today: new haircuts are now available in-game, giving the expedition even more style to strut around in! 💅 

For the full list of changes, fixes, and improvements, you can read the patch notes here

Community Emotes

Our community is packed with phenomenally talented artists and we wanted to celebrate that today.  

We commissioned some of our amazing community creators to design official Expedition 33 emotes for you to use in your own channels! 

A massive thank you to IrunoArt, comickergirl (Sarah Leuver), and Bugyakis for their brilliant work on each of these!!

They're FREE to download and use here

Official Baguette Merch

In the mood to add some baguette to your wardrobe? 

We’ve partnered with Orcival and Le Béret Français to bring you the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 striped shirt and beret for your cosplays! 🥖    You can purchase the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 x Orcival mariniere here

And the official Clair Obscur: Expedition 33 x Le Béret Français beret is available to buy here

On top of that, keep an eye out for a limited number of units of the Monolith Set to be back in stock from our partners at Laced and Pix n' Love soon!! 

And Finally… Cake

It's been a big day for us. Thank you for making it possible. 🎂 

And if you know someone who wants to pick up the game, we're running a 20% sale right now on Steam - As well as some fun merchandise goodies available on our merch page!

Merch Page

From the bottom of our hearts, we’re so thankful to each and every one of you – this has been the best year of our lives, thanks to you. 

 

- The Expedition 33 Team
